items.title: Grammar essentials — tenses, articles, prepositions, agreement
items.body:
The **20-mark grammar MCQ** section (Item 09) rewards a few reliable rules.

**Tenses (time + link):**
- 'since + point' / 'for + period' → present perfect (*has lived since 2015 / for ten years*).
- Action finished before another past action → past perfect (*had left before I arrived*).

**Articles by SOUND, not spelling:**
- a university, a European (consonant /y/ sound); an hour, an honest man (silent h); an MP (vowel sound of 'em').
- 'the' for something specific/unique (*the sun, the Prime Minister*).

**Prepositions (fixed pairs):**

| Word | Prep | Word | Prep |
|---|---|---|---|
| accused | of | married | to |
| charged | with | good | at |
| blamed | for | different | from |

**Subject–verb agreement:**
- 'One of the + plural' → singular verb (*one of the boys **is***).
- Ignore words between the subject and verb.

**Connectives (cohesive devices) — pick by relationship:**

| Relationship | Connective |
|---|---|
| Contrast | however, but, yet, nevertheless |
| Addition | moreover, furthermore, also |
| Result | therefore, so, hence |
| Similarity | similarly, likewise |

*Example:* 'The scheme was well designed; **however**, it failed for want of funds.' (good design versus failure = contrast).
keyPoints: 'since + point' and 'for + period' take the present perfect (has/have + V3).
Choose a/an by sound: an hour, a university, an MP.
Use 'the' for specific or unique things.
Fixed pairs: accused of, charged with, married to, good at, different from.
'One of the + plural noun' takes a singular verb; ignore words between subject and verb.
Connectives: contrast = however; addition = moreover; result = therefore; similarity = similarly.
items.source: APPSC 07/2026 English syllabus — Grammar (Item 09); SSC-standard rules.

items.title: Voice, narration and sentence transformation — conversion rules
items.body:
**Active → Passive:** keep the tense, swap subject/object, add 'by'. Use the right form of 'be' + past participle.

| Active tense | Passive |
|---|---|
| present simple (writes) | is/are written |
| past simple (wrote) | was/were written |
| present perfect (has written) | has/have been written |
| modal (must write) | must be written |

**Direct → Indirect (narration):** back-shift the tense and change time/pronoun words.
- will→would, can→could, may→might; is→was; go→went.
- now→then, today→that day, tomorrow→the next day, here→there.
- Statements use 'that'; questions use 'asked' + (wh-word / if-whether) with normal word order; requests use 'requested + object + to-infinitive'.

**Common transformations:**
- too ... to = so ... that + cannot.
- No sooner ... **than** ...; Hardly ... **when** ...
- 'One of the largest cities' (superlative) = 'Very few cities are as large as ...' (positive).
keyPoints: Passive = correct form of 'be' + past participle, keeping the original tense.
Narration back-shift: will→would, can→could, is→was; now→then, tomorrow→the next day.
Reported questions use 'asked' + wh-/if-whether with statement word order.
'too ... to' = 'so ... that + cannot'.
Correlatives: 'No sooner ... than', 'Hardly ... when'.

items.title: Vocabulary & word-building — synonyms, one-word, affixes, confusables
items.body:
Several MCQ areas reward a strong vocabulary and word-building sense.

**Synonyms/Antonyms:** learn word + meaning + opposite together: *benevolent* = kind, well-meaning (opposite: malevolent, cruel); *candid* = frank (opposite: evasive); *abundant* = plentiful (opposite: scarce).

**One-word substitution:** replace a phrase with one precise term — *bureaucracy* (rule by officials), *illiterate* (cannot read/write), *aviary* (place for birds), *polyglot* (knows many languages).

**Affixes (assimilation):** negative 'in-' becomes **il-** before l (illegal), **ir-** before r (irregular), **im-** before m/p (impossible). Suffix '-less' = without (fearless); '-ful' = full of (careful).

**Phrasal verbs (verb + particle, new meaning):** *call off* = cancel; *put off* = postpone; *carry out* = perform; *look into* = investigate; *give up* = stop. **Don't confuse:** call off (cancel completely) vs put off (move to a later time).

**Idioms:** figurative, not literal — *burn the midnight oil* (study late), *bury the hatchet* (make peace), *at the eleventh hour* (last moment).

**Confusables/homophones:** affect (verb) vs effect (noun); stationary (still) vs stationery (paper); their/there/they're; principal (head) vs principle (rule).

**Administrative glossary:** agenda (items to discuss), minutes (record after), quorum (minimum members), memorandum (note of terms).
keyPoints: Learn synonym/antonym pairs together (benevolent↔malevolent, abundant↔scarce).
One-word substitutions: bureaucracy, illiterate, aviary, polyglot.
Negative 'in-' assimilates: il- before l, ir- before r, im- before m/p.
Idioms are figurative: burn the midnight oil, bury the hatchet, at the eleventh hour.
Confusables: affect(v)/effect(n), stationary/stationery, principal/principle.
Admin terms: agenda vs minutes vs quorum vs memorandum.
Phrasal verbs: call off = cancel; put off = postpone; carry out = perform; look into = investigate.
items.source: SSC-standard English vocabulary (Items 08-14 of grammar list).

items.title: Composition I — formal letter & press release/appeal
items.body:
**Formal letter (Item 02, ~100 words, 10 marks)** — an opinion on an office matter/issue.

Layout: sender's address + date → receiver's designation/address → **Subject** → salutation (*Dear Sir/Madam*) → ¶1 purpose → ¶2 details/opinion → ¶3 courteous request/close → **Yours faithfully** → name.
- Tone: polite, formal, no contractions; purpose in the first line; one idea per paragraph.

**Press release / Appeal (Item 03, ~100 words, 10 marks)** — on a recent concern/problem/disaster/rumour.

Layout: organisation name + **PRESS RELEASE / APPEAL** label → headline → dateline (place, date) → body (most important fact first — *inverted pyramid*) → a spokesperson quote / contact.
- For an appeal: name the cause and the exact help needed; keep it factual and quotable.
keyPoints: Formal letter (~100 words, 10 marks): address, date, Subject, salutation, purpose→details→request, 'Yours faithfully'.
Letter tone is polite and formal with the purpose stated in the first line.
Press release/appeal (~100 words, 10 marks): label + headline + dateline + inverted-pyramid facts + quote/contact.
An appeal must name the cause and the specific help needed.
Both are factual and impersonal — no slang or contractions.

items.title: Composition II — report, visual information & formal speech
items.body:
**Report writing (Item 04, ~150 words, 15 marks)** — of a function/event/field trip/survey.
- Heading + by-line → opening with the **5 Ws** (what, when, where, who, why) → factual details in order → outcome.
- Style: **third person, past tense, objective** — no personal feelings.

**Writing on visual information (Item 05, ~150 words, 15 marks)** — a graph/table/flow-chart/statistics.
- State what the visual shows (title, units, period) → give the **main trend** → key figures and comparisons → notable exceptions.
- **Describe, do not interpret**; no opinions. Use comparison language (higher than, doubled, the largest).

**Formal speech (Item 06, ~150 words, 15 marks)** — inauguration/seminar/ceremony.
- Greeting to audience/dignitaries → introduce the topic → 2-3 points with examples → an appeal → close + thanks.
- Use direct address ('respected guests'), short sentences, a memorable ending.
keyPoints: Report (~150 words, 15 marks): heading + by-line + 5 Ws; third person, past tense, objective.
Visual information (~150 words, 15 marks): state what it shows, give the main trend, key figures — describe, don't interpret.
Use comparison language for visuals (higher than, doubled, the largest); no opinions.
Formal speech (~150 words, 15 marks): greeting, topic, 2-3 points, appeal, close with thanks.
Speech uses direct address and short, memorable sentences.

items.title: The English paper item by item — marks, lengths and the 14 grammar areas
items.body:
**In one line:** the English qualifying paper has **10 items totalling 150 marks**; seven are writing formats with a fixed length, and item 09 is a **20-mark grammar MCQ set drawn from 14 named areas**.

**Why it is asked:** knowing the length and marks of each item tells you how much to write and where the easy marks are.

| Item | Task | Length | Marks |
|---|---|---|---|
| 01 | Essay — one topic from a list of five | 200-250 words | 20 |
| 02 | Formal letter giving an opinion | ~100 words | 10 |
| 03 | Press release / appeal | ~100 words | 10 |
| 04 | Report writing | ~150 words | 15 |
| 05 | Writing on visual information | ~150 words | 15 |
| 06 | Formal speech | ~150 words | 15 |
| 07 | Précis of a 300-word passage | ~100 words | 15 |
| 08 | Reading comprehension | ~250-word passage | 15 |
| 09 | Grammar MCQs | 14 areas | 20 |
| 10 | Translation, regional language → English | ~150 words | 15 |

**Essay (item 01):** the topic may be **descriptive, analytical, philosophical or based on current affairs**; choose **one of five** (the Telugu paper offers one of three).

**The 14 grammar areas of item 09:** tenses; voice; narration (direct-indirect); transformation of sentences; articles and determiners; prepositions; phrasal verbs; idiomatic expressions; **administrative glossary**; synonyms/antonyms; one-word substitution; cohesive devices/connectives/linkers; affixes; words that cause confusion (homonyms/homophones).

**Letter topics named in the syllabus:** daily office matters, a problem that has occurred in the office, or an opinion sought by a ranked officer.
**Press release / appeal topics:** a recent concern, problem, disaster or **rumours**.
**Report topics:** an official function, event, field trip or survey.
**Visual information:** a graph, image, flow chart, table of comparison or simple statistical data.
**Formal speech:** an inauguration, an educational seminar/conference or a formal ceremony.

**Remember it:** *20-10-10-15-15-15-15-15-20-15 = 150.*

**Don't confuse:** the qualifying-paper essay (**200-250 words**, 20 marks) with the Paper-I General Essay (**three essays of ~800 words**).
keyPoints: English qualifying: 10 items = 150 marks; essay 20, letter 10, press release 10, report 15, visual 15, speech 15, précis 15, RC 15, grammar 20, translation 15.
Essay (item 01): 200-250 words, one topic from five; descriptive/analytical/philosophical/current affairs.
Item 09 grammar MCQs (20 marks) come from 14 named areas, including administrative glossary and affixes.
Letter topics: daily office matters, an office problem, or an opinion sought by a ranked officer.
Press release/appeal topics: a recent concern, problem, disaster or rumours.
Visual information: graph, image, flow chart, table of comparison or simple statistical data.
items.source: APPSC Notification 07/2026 — English (Qualifying) items 01-06 & 09; Wren & Martin; SSC-standard English grammar and vocabulary

items.title: Tenses and conditionals — the twelve forms and the signal words
items.body:
**In one line:** English has **3 times × 4 aspects = 12 tense forms**; signal words (since, already, yesterday, by the time) tell you which one a blank needs.

**Why it is asked:** "tenses" is the first of the 14 grammar areas, and error-spotting items usually hinge on one signal word.

| | Simple | Continuous | Perfect | Perfect continuous |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Present | writes | is writing | has written | has been writing |
| Past | wrote | was writing | had written | had been writing |
| Future | will write | will be writing | will have written | will have been writing |

**Signal words:**

| Signal | Tense | Example |
|---|---|---|
| since / for | present perfect (continuous) | has lived here since 2015 |
| already, yet, just, ever | present perfect | I have just finished |
| yesterday, ago, last year | simple past | He left two days ago |
| by the time + past | past perfect | The train had left by the time we arrived |
| every day, usually | simple present | She walks every morning |

**Stative verbs** (know, believe, love, belong, understand) are **not used in the continuous**: *I know him* (not *I am knowing*).

**Conditionals:**

| Type | If-clause | Main clause | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zero | present | present | general truth |
| First | present | will + verb | real future possibility |
| Second | past (were) | would + verb | unreal present |
| Third | past perfect | would have + V3 | unreal past |

- **If I were you** — "were" for all persons in the unreal second conditional.
- **It is high time** + past tense: *It is high time we left.*
- **I wish** + past (present regret) / past perfect (past regret).
- **Lest** takes **should**: *Walk fast lest you should miss the bus.*
- **Unless = if not**, so never add another "not": *Unless you work hard, you will fail.*
- **No future after "when / if"** in time clauses: *I will call you when he comes* (not *will come*).

**Don't confuse:** present perfect (link to now: *has seen*) with simple past (finished time: *saw yesterday*) — "yesterday" never takes the present perfect.
keyPoints: 12 tense forms = 3 times (present, past, future) × 4 aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous).
already/yet/just/ever → present perfect; yesterday/ago/last year → simple past.
"By the time" + past → past perfect (the train had left by the time we arrived).
Stative verbs (know, believe, love, belong) are not used in the continuous.
Conditionals: zero = general truth; first = if + present, will; second = if + past, would; third = if + past perfect, would have + V3.
"If I were"; "It is high time" + past; "lest" + should; "unless" = if not (no extra not).
No future tense after when/if in a time clause: "when he comes".

items.title: More voice and narration rules — imperatives, questions and pronoun changes
items.body:
**In one line:** beyond the basic tense table, voice and narration questions test **imperatives, questions, continuous forms, "by"-alternatives** and the **pronoun and time-word changes** of reported speech.

**Why it is asked:** voice and narration are two of the 14 grammar areas, and each has 6-8 fixed conversion rules.

**Voice — more rules:**

| Active | Passive |
|---|---|
| present continuous: is writing | is being written |
| past continuous: was writing | was being written |
| future: will write | will be written |
| imperative: Open the door. | Let the door be opened. |
| question: Who wrote this? | By whom was this written? |

- **Intransitive verbs** (sleep, go, arrive) have **no object, so no passive**.
- The **agent is dropped** when unknown or obvious: *The thief was caught.*
- Some verbs take a preposition other than *by*: **known to**, **pleased with**, **surprised at**, **interested in**, **filled with**.

**Narration — more rules:**
1. If the reporting verb is in the **present** (*says*), the tense **does not change**.
2. A **universal truth** keeps its tense: *He said that the sun rises in the east.*
3. **Time and place words:** this → that; these → those; yesterday → the previous day; last night → the previous night; ago → before; here → there.
4. **Modals:** shall → should; must → had to; may → might.
5. **Commands:** told / ordered / requested / advised + object + **to-infinitive**; a negative command takes **not to**: *He told me not to go.*
6. **Exclamations:** exclaimed with joy / sorrow: *"What a goal!" → He exclaimed with joy that it was a great goal.*
7. **"Let's"** → **suggested that** they **should**: *He said, "Let's go." → He suggested that they should go.*

**Pronoun rule (SON — 1-2-3):** a **first**-person pronoun changes to match the **Subject** of the reporting verb; a **second**-person pronoun changes to match the **Object**; a **third**-person pronoun does **not** change.

**Don't confuse:** **said to** (keeps the listener: *She said to me*) with **told** (*She told me that …*) — "told that" without a listener is wrong.
keyPoints: Continuous passive: is/was being written; future passive: will be written.
Imperative passive: "Open the door" → "Let the door be opened"; question: "Who wrote this?" → "By whom was this written?"
Intransitive verbs (sleep, go, arrive) have no passive; agents like "known to", "pleased with", "surprised at" replace "by".
Present reporting verb or universal truth → no tense change.
this → that; yesterday → the previous day; last night → the previous night; ago → before; must → had to.
Commands: told/ordered/requested + to-infinitive; negative: not to; "Let's" → suggested that … should.
SON 1-2-3: first person follows the Subject, second follows the Object, third does not change.

items.title: Articles and determiners — when to use the, and few vs a few
items.body:
**In one line:** **a/an** is chosen by **sound**, **the** marks something **specific or unique**, and a short list of name types takes **the** while another list takes **no article**; determiners such as **few / a few** change the meaning completely.

**Why it is asked:** "articles and determiners" is one of the 14 grammar areas; questions test the exceptions.

**"The" is used with:**

| Category | Examples |
|---|---|
| rivers, seas, oceans | the Godavari, the Arabian Sea, the Indian Ocean |
| mountain ranges, groups of islands | the Himalayas, the Andamans |
| deserts | the Thar |
| unique things | the sun, the earth |
| superlatives and ordinals | the best, the first |
| musical instruments | play the veena |
| newspapers and holy books | the Hindu, the Gita |
| the + adjective = a whole class | the rich, the poor |

**No article with:** names of persons and cities; **a single mountain** (Mount Everest); languages (*Telugu is sweet*); meals (*after lunch*); games (*play cricket*); abstract nouns in a general sense (*Honesty is the best policy*). Most countries take no article, **but the USA, the UK and the Netherlands do**.

**Determiners — meaning changes:**

| Determiner | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| few | hardly any (negative) | Few people came — a poor turnout |
| a few | some (positive) | A few people came — enough to start |
| the few | all of the small number | The few books he had were old |
| little / a little | same contrast for uncountables | little hope vs a little hope |
| many / fewer | countable nouns | many cars, fewer cars |
| much / less | uncountable nouns | much water, less water |
| each | one by one, of two or more | each of the two hands |
| every | all, of three or more | every student |

**Remember it:** *few = almost none; a few = some.*

**Don't confuse:** **fewer** (countable: fewer mistakes) with **less** (uncountable: less time).
keyPoints: "The" with rivers, seas, oceans, mountain ranges, groups of islands, deserts, unique things, superlatives, ordinals, instruments, newspapers, holy books.
"The" + adjective = a whole class (the rich, the poor).
No article with persons, cities, a single mountain (Mount Everest), languages, meals, games, general abstract nouns.
Most countries take no article, but the USA, the UK, the Netherlands do.
few = hardly any (negative); a few = some (positive); the few = all of the small number.
many/fewer for countable nouns; much/less for uncountable nouns.
each = one by one (two or more); every = all (three or more).

items.title: Prepositions — time, place and the fixed pairs
items.body:
**In one line:** prepositions of **time and place** follow **at → on → in** (small → large), and many verbs and adjectives take one **fixed** preposition that must be memorised.

**Why it is asked:** "use of prepositions" is one of the 14 grammar areas; error-spotting items swap the fixed preposition.

**Time:**

| Preposition | Used with | Example |
|---|---|---|
| at | a clock time | at 6 o'clock |
| on | a day or date | on Monday, on 15 August |
| in | a month, year, season | in July, in 2026, in summer |
| since | a point of time (perfect tense) | since 2015 |
| for | a period (perfect tense) | for ten years |

**Pairs that confuse:**
- **between** two; **among** more than two.
- **beside** = next to; **besides** = in addition to.
- **by** the agent (*written by Gurajada*); **with** the instrument (*cut with a knife*).
- **die of** a disease (*died of cholera*); **die from** a cause/injury (*died from overwork*).
- **angry with** a person; **angry at** a thing.
- **deal in** = trade in; **deal with** = handle.
- **differ from** (be unlike); **differ with** (disagree with a person).

**Fixed pairs:**

| Word | Preposition | Word | Preposition |
|---|---|---|---|
| abide | by | comply | with |
| adept | in | conducive | to |
| afraid | of | consist | of |
| aim | at | insist | on |
| congratulate | on | prefer | to |
| independent | of | refrain | from |
| superior / inferior | to | rely | on |
| senior / junior | to | preferable | to |
| prior | to | tired | of |

**Remember it:** *Latin comparatives (superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior, preferable) take "to", never "than".*

**Don't confuse:** **prefer A to B** (*I prefer tea to coffee*) with the wrong *prefer A than B*.
keyPoints: at + clock time; on + day/date; in + month/year/season.
between two; among more than two; beside = next to; besides = in addition to.
by + agent; with + instrument; die of a disease; die from a cause.
angry with a person, at a thing; deal in = trade, deal with = handle.
Fixed: abide by, comply with, conducive to, consist of, insist on, refrain from, rely on, independent of, congratulate on.
superior/inferior/senior/junior/prior/preferable + to (never than); prefer A to B.

items.title: Subject-verb agreement and transformation of sentences
items.body:
**In one line:** the verb agrees with the **real** subject (not the nearest noun), and a sentence can be **transformed** between simple/compound/complex, degrees of comparison, affirmative/negative and question/statement **without changing its meaning**.

**Why it is asked:** "transformation of sentences" is one of the 14 areas, and agreement errors are the commonest spot-the-error items.

**Agreement rules:**

| Subject | Verb | Example |
|---|---|---|
| each / every … | singular | Each of the boys **is** ready |
| either / neither (alone) | singular | Neither of them **was** present |
| neither … nor / either … or | agrees with the **nearer** subject | Neither the clerk nor the officers **were** late |
| the number of + plural | singular | The number of cars **is** rising |
| a number of + plural | plural | A number of cars **are** parked |
| X as well as / along with Y | agrees with **X** | The minister, along with his aides, **has** arrived |
| news, mathematics, politics (subject) | singular | The news **is** good |
| scissors, trousers, spectacles | plural | My spectacles **are** broken |
| committee, jury (as one unit) | singular | The jury **has** given its verdict |

**Sentence types by structure:**
- **Simple** — one finite verb: *Being ill, he stayed home.*
- **Compound** — two main clauses joined by **and / but / or / so**: *He was ill, so he stayed home.*
- **Complex** — a main clause + a subordinate clause (**because, when, although, who, that**): *As he was ill, he stayed home.*

**Degrees of comparison:** *Mumbai is the largest city in India* (superlative) = *Mumbai is larger than any other city in India* (comparative) = *No other city in India is as large as Mumbai* (positive).

**Other transformations:**
- Affirmative → negative: *Only he can do it* → *None but he can do it*; *He always comes on time* → *He never fails to come on time*.
- Interrogative → assertive (rhetorical question): *Who does not love his country?* → *Everyone loves his country.*
- Exclamatory → assertive: *What a beautiful day!* → *It is a very beautiful day.*
- *As soon as he came, the meeting began* = *No sooner had he come than the meeting began.*

**Don't confuse:** **the number of** (singular verb) with **a number of** (plural verb).
keyPoints: each/every/either/neither (alone) → singular verb.
neither … nor / either … or → verb agrees with the nearer subject.
the number of → singular; a number of → plural.
"as well as / along with" → verb agrees with the first subject.
news, mathematics → singular; scissors, trousers, spectacles → plural; jury/committee as a unit → singular.
Simple = one finite verb; compound = main clauses joined by and/but/or/so; complex = main + subordinate clause.
Superlative → "larger than any other" → "No other … as large as".
"Only he" → "None but he"; "always" → "never fails to"; "As soon as" → "No sooner … than".
items.source: APPSC Notification 07/2026 — English (Qualifying) items 01-06 & 09; Wren & Martin; SSC-standard English grammar and vocabulary

items.title: Phrasal verbs, idioms, one-word substitutes and synonym pairs
items.body:
**In one line:** these four vocabulary areas are pure recall — a **phrasal verb** is verb + particle with a new meaning, an **idiom** is a fixed figurative phrase, and a **one-word substitute** replaces a whole description.

**Why it is asked:** four of the 14 grammar areas are vocabulary areas; each item is a quick mark if the pair is known.

**Phrasal verbs:**

| Phrasal verb | Meaning | Phrasal verb | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| bring up | raise (a child) / mention | look after | take care of |
| turn down | reject | put up with | tolerate |
| break down | stop working / collapse | take after | resemble a parent |
| set up | establish | run out of | have none left |
| come across | find by chance | look forward to | wait eagerly (+ -ing) |
| make up for | compensate | give in | surrender |

**Idioms:**

| Idiom | Meaning |
|---|---|
| a bolt from the blue | a complete surprise |
| beat about the bush | avoid the main point |
| hit the nail on the head | say exactly the right thing |
| a white elephant | a costly, useless possession |
| red tape | excessive official formality |
| cry over spilt milk | regret what cannot be undone |
| a feather in one's cap | an achievement to be proud of |
| in hot water | in trouble |
| once in a blue moon | very rarely |
| spill the beans | reveal a secret |
| break the ice | start a conversation |
| at loggerheads | in strong disagreement |
| Achilles' heel | a weak point |
| a red-letter day | a memorable, happy day |

**One-word substitution:**

| Description | One word |
|---|---|
| rule by a single person with absolute power | autocracy |
| absence of government | anarchy |
| rule by the wealthy | plutocracy |
| rule by religious leaders | theocracy |
| one who knows everything | omniscient |
| present everywhere | omnipresent |
| one who loves mankind and gives to help | philanthropist |
| one who hates mankind | misanthrope |
| lover of books | bibliophile |
| unable to pay debts | insolvent |
| born / published after the father's or author's death | posthumous |
| with everyone agreeing | unanimous |
| disease spreading over a whole country or the world | pandemic |
| a false name used by an author | pseudonym |
| cannot be read | illegible |
| fit to be eaten | edible |
| spoken without preparation | extempore |
| a remedy for all ills | panacea |
| place where dead bodies are kept | mortuary |
| place for storing grain | granary |
| place for keeping bees | apiary |
| killing of one's king | regicide |

**Synonym / antonym pairs:** candid = frank (× evasive); abundant = plentiful (× scarce); obstinate = stubborn (× flexible); transparent = clear (× opaque); diligent = hard-working (× lazy); frugal = thrifty (× extravagant).

**Don't confuse:** **omniscient** (all-knowing) with **omnipotent** (all-powerful) and **omnipresent** (everywhere).
keyPoints: turn down = reject; put up with = tolerate; take after = resemble; run out of = have none left; come across = find by chance.
set up = establish; make up for = compensate; give in = surrender; look forward to + -ing.
a bolt from the blue = a surprise; beat about the bush = avoid the point; a white elephant = costly, useless possession; red tape = official delay.
once in a blue moon = very rarely; spill the beans = reveal a secret; at loggerheads = in disagreement; Achilles' heel = weak point.
autocracy = rule by one; anarchy = no government; plutocracy = rule by the rich; theocracy = rule by religious leaders.
omniscient = all-knowing; philanthropist × misanthrope; insolvent = unable to pay debts; posthumous = after death; unanimous = all agreeing.
illegible = cannot be read; edible = fit to eat; extempore = without preparation; panacea = cure-all; apiary = bees; granary = grain.
candid × evasive; abundant × scarce; frugal × extravagant; diligent × lazy; transparent × opaque.

items.title: Administrative glossary, confusable words, affixes and linkers
items.body:
**In one line:** the **administrative glossary** is the Latin and official vocabulary of government files; **confusables** are look-alike or sound-alike words; **affixes** build new words; **linkers** show how ideas relate.

**Why it is asked:** "administrative glossary" is named in the syllabus because a Group-I officer writes notes and orders; the other three areas are classic error items.

**Administrative glossary:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ad hoc | for a particular purpose only, temporary |
| ex officio | by virtue of one's office |
| bona fide | genuine, in good faith |
| sine die | without fixing a date (adjourned indefinitely) |
| suo motu | on its own motion, without a petition |
| ultra vires | beyond one's legal powers |
| prima facie | at first sight |
| pro rata | in proportion |
| status quo | the existing state of affairs |
| in camera | in private, not in open court |
| de facto / de jure | in fact / by law |
| ex gratia | as a favour, not as a legal duty |
| inter alia | among other things |
| sub judice | under judicial consideration |
| circular | an order sent to many offices at once |
| ordinance | a law made by the executive when the legislature is not in session |
| affidavit | a written statement on oath |

**Confusable words:**

| Pair | Meaning |
|---|---|
| complement / compliment | completes / praise |
| council / counsel | a body / advice or a lawyer |
| accept / except | receive / leave out |
| loose / lose | not tight / misplace |
| eminent / imminent | distinguished / about to happen |
| elicit / illicit | draw out / illegal |
| adverse / averse | unfavourable / unwilling |
| canvas / canvass | cloth / seek votes |
| discreet / discrete | careful / separate |
| personal / personnel | private / staff |
| precede / proceed | come before / go on |
| ensure / insure | make certain / protect by insurance |

**Affixes:** prefixes **un-** (unhappy), **dis-** (disagree), **mis-** (misuse), **non-** (non-violent), **anti-** (anti-social), **pre-** (pre-war), **post-** (post-war), **re-** (rewrite); suffixes **-ness / -ment / -tion** make nouns (kindness, development, action), **-able / -ful / -less** make adjectives, **-ize** makes verbs (modernize), **-ly** makes adverbs.

**Linkers (cohesive devices):**

| Relationship | Linkers |
|---|---|
| condition | unless, provided that, in case |
| concession | although, even though, despite |
| cause | because, since, as, owing to |
| purpose | so that, in order to |
| example | for instance, such as |
| summary | in short, to sum up |
| sequence | first, then, finally |

**Don't confuse:** **despite** (no "of": *despite the rain*) with **in spite of** (*in spite of the rain*).
keyPoints: ad hoc = temporary, for one purpose; ex officio = by virtue of office; bona fide = genuine; sine die = without a date.
suo motu = on its own motion; ultra vires = beyond legal powers; prima facie = at first sight; pro rata = in proportion.
status quo = existing state; in camera = in private; de facto / de jure = in fact / by law; ex gratia = as a favour; sub judice = before a court.
ordinance = executive law when the legislature is not in session; affidavit = statement on oath; circular = order sent to many offices.
complement/compliment; council/counsel; eminent/imminent; elicit/illicit; adverse/averse; personal/personnel; precede/proceed.
Prefixes un-, dis-, mis-, non-, anti-, pre-, post-, re-; suffixes -ness/-ment/-tion (nouns), -ize (verbs), -ly (adverbs).
Linkers: condition = unless/provided that; concession = although/despite; cause = because/owing to; purpose = so that.

items.title: Composition formats — closings, press-release conventions, charts and speeches
items.body:
**In one line:** each writing format has a few **conventions** that examiners check first — the letter's closing, the press release's label and end mark, the chart's trend language, and the speech's order of address.

**Why it is asked:** format marks are easy marks; a missing "Subject" line or "Yours sincerely" to "Sir" costs marks.

**Formal letter (item 02):**
- **Dear Sir / Madam** → **Yours faithfully** (the reader is not known by name).
- **Dear Mr Rao** (named) → **Yours sincerely**.
- Include a **Subject:** line; state the purpose in the first line; no contractions.

**Press release (item 03):**
- Starts with **FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE** (or PRESS RELEASE), a **headline** and a **dateline** (city, date).
- **Inverted pyramid** — the most important fact first.
- A quote from a spokesperson, a contact line, and an end mark **### or ENDS**.
- An **appeal** names the cause, the exact help needed and how to give it.

**Report (item 04):** heading + **by-line** ("by a staff reporter"); 5 Ws; **past tense, third person**, often **passive** (*The function was inaugurated by …*). A **survey report** has **purpose → method → findings → recommendations**.

**Visual information (item 05):**

| Visual | Best for |
|---|---|
| line graph | a trend over time |
| bar chart | comparing quantities |
| pie chart | parts of a whole (percentages) |
| table | exact figures side by side |
| flow chart | stages of a process |

Trend language: *rose sharply, declined steadily, peaked at, remained stable, fluctuated*. Structure: **introduction (what it shows) → overview (main trend) → details (figures) → summary**.

**Formal speech (item 06):** address in order of rank — *Honourable Chief Guest, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen* → introduce the occasion → 2-3 points → appeal → thanks. A **welcome address** opens a function; a **vote of thanks** closes it by thanking the chief guest, organisers and audience.

**Don't confuse:** **Yours faithfully** (unnamed reader) with **Yours sincerely** (named reader).
keyPoints: Dear Sir/Madam → Yours faithfully; Dear Mr Rao → Yours sincerely; include a Subject line.
Press release: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE, headline, dateline, inverted pyramid, quote, contact, ends with ### or ENDS.
Report: heading + by-line, 5 Ws, past tense, third person, often passive; survey report = purpose, method, findings, recommendations.
Line graph = trend over time; bar chart = comparison; pie chart = parts of a whole; flow chart = stages of a process.
Trend words: rose sharply, declined steadily, peaked, remained stable, fluctuated.
Speech: address dignitaries in order of rank; welcome address opens, vote of thanks closes a function.
